vignette:
At 48, she speaks with the practiced calm of someone used to sitting beside other people’s pain. She works in social ministry, the kind of job that asks her to visit hospital rooms, organize meals, pray with families when they want prayer, and help people endure the ordinary devastations of illness, poverty, and grief. Before the accident, she describes herself as steady, capable, and hard to rattle. She lives alone, keeps a small apartment neat, and has built a life around showing up for others. She says that for years she believed that if she stayed grounded enough, compassionate enough, she could move through almost anything.

The accident happens on a wet afternoon as she is driving home after visiting an older parishioner. She remembers the light changing, the blur of rain on the windshield, and then a truck sliding through the intersection too fast. She has a sharp, impossible thought—This is how I die—just before the impact. Metal folds in around her. The sound is enormous. For a few seconds, maybe longer, she cannot breathe properly and cannot tell where her body ends and the crushed car begins. She smells gasoline and something burnt. She is sure the car will catch fire. She cannot get her door open. She screams for help, then hears herself screaming as if from far away. Later, she remembers a stranger’s face at the window and the pressure of the seatbelt cutting into her chest. What stays with her most is the helplessness: being fully awake, knowing she may be killed, and being unable to move.

She survives with multiple injuries that heal better on paper than they do in her mind. In the first weeks after the accident, everyone tells her how lucky she is. She repeats that word—lucky—because it is what people need to hear. She sends thank-you texts from her bed, posts a brief message asking for prayers, and tries to sound like herself. But at night she jerks awake with her heart racing, convinced for an instant that she is trapped again. She hears the crunch of metal as she is falling asleep. Sometimes she smells gasoline in her apartment and walks from room to room checking the stove, the outlets, the windows, although she knows the smell is not real.

When she is physically able to return to work, she expects routine and faith to carry her back. Instead, the world feels newly dangerous and unpredictable. Riding in a car makes her grip the door handle until her hand cramps. At red lights she watches cross traffic with such intensity that she stops hearing the person beside her. If a vehicle approaches too fast, her whole body seizes; she ducks, gasps, or shouts before she can stop herself. She starts leaving absurdly early so she can avoid rain, highways, and busy intersections. Then she begins avoiding certain visits altogether if they require unfamiliar routes. She tells colleagues she is overloaded, which is partly true.

The worst moments come uninvited. A screech of brakes outside the church throws her straight back into the intersection, heart pounding, skin cold, as if the accident is happening again in the present tense. During pastoral visits, while someone is telling her about a dying husband or an addicted son, an image flashes into her mind—the buckled hood, shattered glass, the thought of burning alive—and she has to work to keep her face composed. She feels ashamed of this. Her work has always depended on being present, and now she finds herself scanning exits, windows, traffic outside. She prays with people about trust and surrender while privately feeling betrayed by her own nervous system.

She has become more withdrawn since the crash. Friends invite her out, but she often declines if it means riding with someone else or being on the road after dark. She used to stop for groceries on the way home, chat with neighbors, linger after services. Now she goes straight home and locks the door behind her. She sits in silence, exhausted by a day that contains no visible emergency. She keeps telling herself to be grateful, to get over it, to remember that others have survived worse. That inner scolding only deepens her sense of failure.

She also notices how much the accident has changed the way she thinks about herself and the world. She no longer feels basically safe. She does not trust ordinary moments the way she once did; any intersection can become a catastrophe, any routine drive a last drive. She is harsher with herself, embarrassed by how frightened she still is months later. Sometimes she wonders whether the calm, competent woman people relied on was thinner than she believed. She hates that she now startles when someone knocks unexpectedly at her office door, hates that rain on the windshield can make her chest tighten before she is even fully aware of why.

In session, she tells the story carefully, then apologizes for crying. She says she is used to being the one who listens. What emerges over time is not only fear but grief: grief for the sense of safety she had, grief for the ease with which she used to move through her days, grief for the part of her work that felt effortless and openhearted. She still shows up for people. She still brings casseroles, sits at hospital bedsides, and answers late calls. But now she does these things while carrying an invisible intersection inside her, one she keeps reentering even when she is outwardly standing still.
